title: A vocabulary for transparency and depth
description: Words about transparency can describe what is visible without claiming how a material is made.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: Words about transparency can describe what is visible without claiming how a material is made. Start with the image's observable layers.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Describe whether background shapes can be seen, whether edges appear clear or cloudy and where colour seems concentrated. Compare a whole-object view with a detail. Use phrases such as “appears translucent in this image” when the evidence is only photographic.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A blue channel may show lighter areas near an edge and darker areas in its centre. That is an observation about the image, not a measurement of depth or a formula.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: What can be seen through the surface?
Which words describe appearance rather than properties?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: An image cannot certify composition, clarity, ageing behaviour or performance. Confirm material details separately.

title: Reading reflections in a material photograph
description: Reflections can reveal viewing conditions while also disguising surface details.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: Reflections can reveal viewing conditions while also disguising surface details. Reading them carefully helps avoid confusing the room reflected in a surface with the surface itself.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Identify bright shapes that may come from windows or lights. Compare their direction with nearby features. Look for another angle before describing a mark as part of the material. If uncertain, record both interpretations and request clarification.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A pale stripe across a dark top might be a window reflection rather than a coloured band. Naming it as a reflection candidate keeps the brief accurate.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: A photograph cannot establish gloss level, scratch resistance or surface condition with certainty. Do not diagnose a defect from a single reflected highlight.

title: Separating timber grain from screen colour
description: Grain-like pattern and screen colour are separate observations.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: Grain-like pattern and screen colour are separate observations. A reference can communicate the rhythm of a pattern even when its displayed colour is unreliable.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Describe line direction, contrast and spacing before naming a hue. Record which of these matters most. Compare the same reference at whole-object and detail scale. Avoid assigning a timber species unless a reliable source identifies it.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A sweeping pattern may be the attraction even if the warm brown shown on one screen looks cooler on another. The brief can prioritise pattern while leaving colour confirmation open.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: Is pattern or colour the priority?
What scale is the detail shown at?
What material information needs a source?

paragraphs: Screen images do not identify species, provenance, finish or an exact colour match. Those belong in the confirmed specification.

title: Comparing a macro image with a whole-object view
description: A macro image explains a detail; a whole-object view explains where that detail belongs.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: A macro image explains a detail; a whole-object view explains where that detail belongs. Pairing them prevents a small feature from being mistaken for the dominant appearance.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Label the detail's location on the wider image. Compare its visual importance from near and far. Note whether the close-up exaggerates texture, contrast or depth relative to normal viewing. Keep both views in the reference set with different captions.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A gold-coloured fleck may dominate a close-up yet be subtle across the object. The brief should say whether that subtlety or prominence is desired.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: How prominent is it in the whole?
Does the close-up change the intended emphasis?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: A close-up does not establish the physical size of a feature unless a trustworthy scale reference is provided.

title: Why a visual reference is not a material certificate
description: A visual reference and a material certificate answer different questions.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: A visual reference and a material certificate answer different questions. The first can show an appearance; the second must come from an appropriate source and identify what it covers.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: For each reference, write one visible observation and one claim it cannot support. Keep documents about material identity or testing separate from mood images. If a property matters to the intended use, ask what evidence is available for the actual proposed material and finish.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A glossy blue surface can suggest a colour direction. It cannot establish heat resistance, food-contact suitability or a certification simply because an image includes a cup.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: What does the image actually show?
What evidence would answer that question?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: Do not create performance claims from props, filenames or generated imagery. Unverified properties remain questions.

title: Describing a polished surface without assuming its specification
description: A polished-looking surface can be described without guessing its finish system.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: A polished-looking surface can be described without guessing its finish system. Focus on how light and surrounding shapes appear in the image.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Note whether reflections look sharp or diffuse and whether the edge reads as continuous or interrupted. Compare more than one angle if available. State which visual quality you prefer, then ask how the proposed finish would be specified and reviewed.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: “I prefer a calm, continuous reflection” is a visual preference. “This has a particular coating” is a technical claim that requires a source.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.

title: Questions to ask when a finish looks different in two photographs
description: Different photographs can show the same surface differently because the viewing conditions differ.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: Different photographs can show the same surface differently because the viewing conditions differ. Begin by comparing the conditions before deciding the finish has changed.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: List the light source, camera angle, surrounding colours and image crop where known. Mark unknowns rather than filling them in. Ask for a contextual view or clarification tied to the actual piece. Keep the preferred appearance separate from a claim about what caused the difference.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A warm room light and a daylight window can produce different-looking photographs. The useful request is for clarification under relevant conditions, not an automatic demand to reproduce one screenshot.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: Which view is relevant to the intended placement?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: Do not diagnose a material problem or promise a colour match from this comparison.

title: Recording material preferences in plain language
description: Plain language can produce a more useful material discussion than uncertain technical terms.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: Plain language can produce a more useful material discussion than uncertain technical terms. Describe the visual relationship you want before attempting to name a process.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Write observations in pairs: clear beside opaque, fine pattern beside broad colour, quiet edge beside a stronger centre. Rank the pairs by importance. Add a reference for each and explain what part of the reference matters. Leave composition and performance as separate questions.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A request for “a restrained blue accent beside visible grain” communicates a direction without claiming a resin formula, timber species or finishing technique.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: Descriptive language supports a brief but does not replace an agreed material specification or care instructions.

title: What a reference detail leaves outside the frame
description: A cropped detail can hide scale, supports and the surrounding room.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: A cropped detail can hide scale, supports and the surrounding room. Before using it as the main reference, list what lies outside the frame.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Pair the crop with a wider view where available. Mark the area shown and identify missing context. Decide whether the detail is being used for colour, edge shape or another specific reason. Avoid treating absent information as evidence that a feature does not exist.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A close-up of a waterfall-like corner may omit the base and opposite side. It cannot establish the whole object's construction or whether the same detail repeats.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: Missing context remains unknown. Do not invent hidden structure or an unseen installation to complete the story.

title: Building a material discussion from observations
description: A material discussion becomes clearer when observations, preferences and questions are kept apart.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: A material discussion becomes clearer when observations, preferences and questions are kept apart. This allows the atelier to respond to the actual intention rather than to an unsupported technical assumption.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Create a three-row note for each reference. First describe what is visible. Then say what you like about it. Finally ask what would need confirmation for your proposed use. Use the same format for competing references so their differences are easy to compare.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: “Blue area beside brown grain-like lines” is an observation. “I prefer a narrow colour accent” is a preference. “Which material and finish suit this use?” is the question.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: What must be confirmed for the intended use?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: This method does not verify properties or feasibility. It prepares an honest starting point for that discussion.

paragraphs: Keep the resulting note with your current brief. Before sending it, check that it explains one decision clearly and does not turn a preference into an agreed detail. Use the current linked page for the relevant website guidance, and bring any piece-specific uncertainty to the atelier.
